Verify Now Blog > Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS by: Mila Sep 14,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout ESD protection esd protection circuit Previous articles have covered key technologies related to chip ESD, including ESD diodes, power clamps, CDM mechanisms, and ESD testing procedures, with a focus on chip-level electrostatic discharge protection. However, a common problem in real-world engineering applications is that an IC may pass all standard ESD tests but still suffer damage or failure when used on an actual customer circuit board. Engineers often assume that the problem is insufficient chip-level ESD protection. However, this judgment has limitations. Not all electrical failures are caused by ESD. In many real-world applications, the underlying cause may instead be EOS (Electrical Overstress). 1. What Is EOS? EOS stands for Electrical Overstress. It refers to a condition in which an IC is subjected to voltage, current, or power stress beyond its designed safe operating limits, resulting in electrical abnormalities or physical damage. Common EOS Scenarios EOS can occur in many real-world application conditions, including: Power supply overvoltage I/O input voltage exceeding the specified limit Output short circuits Hot-plugging transients Line surge events Power supply reversal Negative voltage stress Ground bounce Abnormal power sequencing EOS is not a single standardized failure test model. Instead, it is a general term for failures caused by excessive electrical stress. Any voltage, current, or power stress that exceeds the device's designed tolerance can potentially result in EOS failure. 2. Key Differences Between EOS and ESD Both ESD and EOS can cause electrical damage to an IC, which is why they are easily confused in engineering practice. However, they differ significantly in terms of stress characteristics, duration, energy, and failure mechanisms. （Comparison of ESD and EOS Waveforms） 3. Why Can an IC Fail After Passing ESD Tests? Passing standardized HBM and CDM tests only demonstrates that an IC can withstand specific short-duration electrostatic discharge stresses under defined test conditions. It does not mean that the device can withstand every type of electrical transient that may occur in a real system. Standard ESD Tests Have Limited Coverage Standard ESD tests are designed around defined test models and conditions. They verify whether an IC's ESD protection structures and discharge paths can safely handle specified electrostatic pulses. However, these tests cannot reproduce every electrical stress that may occur after the IC is integrated into a complete circuit board. Real-World Applications Introduce Different Electrical Stress In actual circuit board applications, electrical stress may come from: Cable insertion and removal Power-on overshoot External load short circuits Surge coupling through long cables Back-EMF from motors, relays, and other inductive loads Transient ground potential rise Abnormal sequencing between multiple power domains Accidental power connection Compared with standardized ESD pulses, these events may have longer durations, higher accumulated energy, or repeated stress characteristics, resulting in different types of IC damage. The internal ESD protection circuit of an IC is primarily designed to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses. Its purpose is to establish a controlled discharge path and divert transient energy. Therefore, passing ESD tests does not mean that an IC has system-level protection against all EOS conditions. （ESD Test PASS vs Real PCB FAIL） 4. The Functional Limits of Internal ESD Protection A common misconception in system design is that an IC can withstand all external electrical disturbances simply because its pins include an ESD protection circuit. In practice, this assumption can create significant reliability risks. What Is Internal ESD Protection Designed For? The internal ESD protection structure is an important protection layer against electrostatic events. It is designed to provide a low-impedance path for short-duration ESD currents and prevent excessive voltage from reaching sensitive internal circuits. However, this protection is not intended to absorb large amounts of energy for an extended period. It should therefore not be treated as a substitute for system-level EOS protection. What Happens Under Sustained Overvoltage? For example, if an I/O pin is continuously exposed to a voltage beyond its specified operating range and the internal protection structure enters conduction, current may continue to flow into or through the IC. As the stress continues, the protection device and related circuits can generate significant heat. Depending on the electrical stress and internal current path, this may eventually cause damage to components such as: I/O protection devices Output driver circuits Power clamp structures Metal interconnects Vias PN junctions Core input circuits The actual damage location depends on the magnitude and duration of the external stress as well as the current path inside the IC. Why Board-Level Protection Is Required A key engineering principle is that internal ESD protection is primarily intended to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses, while system-level electrical stress with significant energy should be limited and protected at the board level. Common board-level protection methods include: TVS devices Series current-limiting resistors Power clamps Fuses Overcurrent protection Appropriate grounding Proper PCB layout The goal is not simply to add more protection components, but to limit the voltage, current, and energy that can reach the IC and provide a controlled path for transient energy. （Board-Level Protection + IC Internal ESD Protection） 5. Typical EOS Damage Locations and Failure Analysis EOS damage is closely related to the actual current path created by the electrical stress. Different types of stress can affect different areas of the IC: Power supply overvoltage: May damage power clamp structures, internal power circuits, metal interconnects, and thin gate-oxide devices. I/O input overvoltage: May damage I/O protection structures, input circuits, pull-up or pull-down protection structures, and core gate circuits. Output short circuit: May damage output driver circuits, metal interconnects, vias, and local diffusion regions. Negative voltage stress: May damage I/O protection structures, junction regions, and input/output circuits. Therefore, EOS failure analysis should not rely solely on the appearance of a localized burn mark. It is more important to trace the source of the electrical stress, current entry and exit paths, stress duration, and energy to identify the root cause. 6. Engineering Differences Between ESD and EOS Failure Signatures There is no absolute method for distinguishing ESD from EOS based solely on physical failure signatures. However, practical failure analysis often reveals some characteristic differences that can be used as initial clues. Common ESD failure characteristics include: Localized single-point damage Gate-oxide breakdown Abnormalities around I/O protection structures Localized PN-junction leakage Leakage or parameter changes at a single pin Common EOS failure characteristics include: More obvious thermal damage Localized melting or burning of metal Significant thermal damage to vias or metal interconnects Large-area circuit damage Abnormalities along power paths Damage to output driver circuits Simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins or circuit nodes It is important to note that these failure signatures are only supporting evidence and should not be treated as final conclusions. Accurate differentiation between ESD and EOS failures requires comprehensive analysis of the failure scenario, electrical test data, application environment, test conditions, damage location, and physical analysis results. 7. The Risks of Misdiagnosing EOS as ESD In real-world applications, misdiagnosing an EOS failure as insufficient ESD protection can lead to an incorrect corrective strategy, wasting design resources while leaving the actual problem unresolved. When an IC is damaged by system-level EOS, simply increasing the size of the internal ESD protection structure, strengthening the internal power clamp, or widening internal metal interconnects generally cannot solve the system-level failure. The root cause may instead be related to board-level electrical stress, such as excessive external surge energy, improper TVS selection, continuous power supply overvoltage, load short circuits, abnormal hot-plug timing, or the lack of an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path for inductive loads. The key risk of misdiagnosing EOS is that engineers may continue to optimize the chip's ESD protection circuit without addressing the actual source and energy path of the system-level electrical stress. As a result, the same failure may occur repeatedly. Therefore, when investigating electrical failures in real-world applications, both chip-level and system-level factors should be considered rather than focusing only on the internal ESD structure. 8. Key Questions for Troubleshooting Suspected EOS Failures When an IC experiences an electrical failure, the following factors can be checked first to avoid automatically classifying the problem as an ESD failure: Failure Scenario Did the failure occur during a standard ESD test or during actual customer operation? Did it occur at the moment of power-up, during cable insertion or removal, after a load short circuit, or when a motor or relay was activated? Failure Location Is the problem limited to leakage at a single I/O pin, a low-resistance path between the power supply and ground, or simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins? Has the overall operating current of the IC changed significantly? Stress Characteristics Was the failure caused by a short-duration transient pulse, continuous overvoltage, or overcurrent? Was there any periodic or repeated electrical stress or abnormal power sequencing? Board-Level Protection Does the circuit board include TVS or other surge protection? Is an appropriate current-limiting circuit provided? Does the power supply have overvoltage or clamping protection? Does the grounding path provide sufficiently low impedance? Does the inductive load have an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path? These factors can help determine whether the failure is related to system-level EOS and provide a basis for tracing the electrical stress path into the IC. Conclusion Both ESD and EOS can cause IC leakage, short circuits, functional abnormalities, and physical damage, but their stress characteristics, protection strategies, and corrective measures are significantly different. Passing standard ESD tests only verifies the IC's ability to withstand specific short-duration electrostatic pulses and does not cover every overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, power reversal, or ground-bounce condition that may occur in a real system. Therefore, when investigating an IC failure in an actual application, engineers should not determine the root cause solely based on the fact that the device passed ESD testing or on the appearance of localized physical damage. Instead, the failure scenario, electrical stress, failure location, current path, board-level protection, and physical analysis results should be considered together. For electrical stress outside standard ESD test conditions, such as overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, and inductive load transients, EOS should be considered as a potential root cause. Appropriate board-level protection can help limit the voltage, current, and energy reaching the IC and reduce the risk of application-level failure.
